true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Redefining `self.downsize` overwrites the 5-argument version

Ruby does not support method overloading by arity. Defining `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` on line 149 overwrites `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` defined on line 145. Any existing caller passing `(from, to, max_width, max_height)` (or 5 arguments with `opts`) will either pass `max_height` as `opts` (causing `TypeError: no implicit conversion of Symbol into Integer` when `opts[:allow_animation]` is accessed) or raise `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (5 for 3..4)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling cache key uses non-deterministic `hash()` and caches across test cases

In `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (line 27) and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 73), the shared cache key is constructed with Python's built-in `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. Because `PYTHONHASHSEED` is randomized per process by default, different worker processes will compute different cache keys for the same `(organization_id, project_ids)`, so `invalidate_upsampling_cache` called in one worker will fail to invalidate entries written by other workers, and different project ID tuples can collide under a 64-bit hash. In addition, caching this in `sentry.utils.cache` (when `sentry.options` already caches option values in memory/Redis) causes stale cache hits in tests when `options.get` is mocked across requests for the same projects. Either rely on `sentry.options`'s built-in caching directly, or use a deterministic representation (e.g. a comma-joined sorted list or SHA-256 digest) for the cache key.

`upsampled_count` sums `sample_weight` without handling NULL/0 values for unsampled events

`upsampled_count` is defined as `Function("toInt64", [Function("sum", [Column("sample_weight")])], alias)`. In Snuba's errors/discover schema, events ingested without client error sampling (or historical events ingested before `sample_weight` was populated) have `sample_weight` as `NULL` or `0` rather than `1.0`. Summing `sample_weight` directly means unsampled events contribute `0` to the count instead of `1` (e.g., a bucket containing only unsampled events will report a count of `0`). Use `ifNull(if(greater(sample_weight, 0), sample_weight, 1), 1)` (or `greatest(sample_weight, 1)`) inside the sum so each unsampled event still counts as 1.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`zip(error_ids, events.values())` can pair event IDs with the wrong nodestore data

`fetch_error_details` calls `events = nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` and then iterates `for event_id, data in zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi` returns a dict keyed by `node_id` whose key order and completeness are not guaranteed to match `node_ids` (for example, some backends omit missing keys or return results in arbitrary order). Pairing `error_ids` positionally with `events.values()` can associate an `event_id` with another event's payload or silently drop events. Iterate over `zip(error_ids, node_ids)` and look up `events.get(node_id)` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Calling `commit` from a background thread violates Arroyo/confluent-kafka thread safety

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background `commit_thread` that calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes the Arroyo `Commit` callback passed into `create_with_partitions`. In Arroyo's `StreamProcessor`, that callback calls `self.__consumer.stage_positions(...)` and `self.__consumer.commit(...)` on the underlying `KafkaConsumer` (and `confluent_kafka.Consumer`), while the main processor thread is concurrently calling `poll()` / `stage_positions()` on the same consumer and unsynchronized internal dicts (`__PartitionState.__staged_offsets`). Arroyo strategies are expected to invoke `commit` from `poll()`, `submit()`, or `join()` on the main consumer thread. Calling `commit` from a separate thread introduces data races on Arroyo's offset state and concurrent calls into the librdkafka consumer.

Work queues are unbounded and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`, allowing unbounded memory growth

In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each `queue.Queue()` is created with `maxsize=0` (unbounded), and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` never raises Arroyo's `MessageRejected`. Although the class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", the main consumer loop will read from Kafka at full speed and buffer an arbitrary number of `WorkItem` objects (each retaining the raw `Message` and decoded payload) in memory if any worker falls behind, risking OOM kills and also failing to flush remaining queued items on shutdown because `worker.shutdown = True` causes workers to exit their loop on the next iteration instead of draining the queue.

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before draining, dropping queued items and skipping final commit

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all workers and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run` checks `while not self.shutdown:`, any worker that finishes its current item sees `self.shutdown == True` and exits immediately instead of draining the remaining items in `work_queue` (which `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is meant to allow). Furthermore, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops `commit_thread` before calling `queue_pool.shutdown()` and never performs a final commit afterwards, so offsets for items completed during shutdown are never committed.

`close()` and `terminate()` shut down the shared `FixedQueuePool`, breaking partition rebalances

`ResultsStrategyFactory` creates a single `self.queue_pool` in `__init__` and reuses it across every `create_with_partitions` call. false_positives.candidate:
Calling `commit` from a background thread violates Arroyo/confluent-kafka thread safety

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background `commit_thread` that calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes the Arroyo `Commit` callback passed into `create_with_partitions`. In Arroyo's `StreamProcessor`, that callback calls `self.__consumer.stage_positions(...)` and `self.__consumer.commit(...)` on the underlying `KafkaConsumer` (and `confluent_kafka.Consumer`), while the main processor thread is concurrently calling `poll()` / `stage_positions()` on the same consumer and unsynchronized internal dicts (`__PartitionState.__staged_offsets`). Arroyo strategies are expected to invoke `commit` from `poll()`, `submit()`, or `join()` on the main consumer thread. Calling `commit` from a separate thread introduces data races on Arroyo's offset state and concurrent calls into the librdkafka consumer.

`close()` and `terminate()` shut down the shared `FixedQueuePool`, breaking partition rebalances

`ResultsStrategyFactory` creates a single `self.queue_pool` in `__init__` and reuses it across every `create_with_partitions` call. In Arroyo, whenever partitions are revoked or rebalanced, the active strategy has `close()`/`join()` (or `terminate()`) called on it, and `create_with_partitions` is then called again to build a new strategy instance. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` and `terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (which permanently shuts down all queues and stops all worker threads), the first rebalance will leave `self.queue_pool` dead: subsequent `submit()` calls on the newly created strategy will raise `queue.ShutDown` (caught and immediately marked completed in `submit()`), silently dropping all messages and committing their offsets without processing.

Work queues are unbounded and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`, allowing unbounded memory growth

In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each `queue.Queue()` is created with `maxsize=0` (unbounded), and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` never raises Arroyo's `MessageRejected`. Although the class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", the main consumer loop will read from Kafka at full speed and buffer an arbitrary number of `WorkItem` objects (each retaining the raw `Message` and decoded payload) in memory if any worker falls behind, risking OOM kills and also failing to flush remaining queued items on shutdown because `worker.shutdown = True` causes workers to exit their loop on the next iteration instead of draining the queue.

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before draining, dropping queued items and skipping final commit

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all workers and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run` checks `while not self.shutdown:`, any worker that finishes its current item sees `self.shutdown == True` and exits immediately instead of draining the remaining items in `work_queue` (which `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is meant to allow). Furthermore, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops `commit_thread` before calling `queue_pool.shutdown()` and never performs a final commit afterwards, so offsets for items completed during shutdown are never committed.

false_positives.candidate:
Calling `commit` from a background thread violates Arroyo/confluent-kafka thread safety

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background `commit_thread` that calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes the Arroyo `Commit` callback passed into `create_with_partitions`. In Arroyo's `StreamProcessor`, that callback calls `self.__consumer.stage_positions(...)` and `self.__consumer.commit(...)` on the underlying `KafkaConsumer` (and `confluent_kafka.Consumer`), while the main processor thread is concurrently calling `poll()` / `stage_positions()` on the same consumer and unsynchronized internal dicts (`__PartitionState.__staged_offsets`). Arroyo strategies are expected to invoke `commit` from `poll()`, `submit()`, or `join()` on the main consumer thread. Calling `commit` from a separate thread introduces data races on Arroyo's offset state and concurrent calls into the librdkafka consumer.

`close()` and `terminate()` shut down the shared `FixedQueuePool`, breaking partition rebalances

`ResultsStrategyFactory` creates a single `self.queue_pool` in `__init__` and reuses it across every `create_with_partitions` call. In Arroyo, whenever partitions are revoked or rebalanced, the active strategy has `close()`/`join()` (or `terminate()`) called on it, and `create_with_partitions` is then called again to build a new strategy instance. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` and `terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (which permanently shuts down all queues and stops all worker threads), the first rebalance will leave `self.queue_pool` dead: subsequent `submit()` calls on the newly created strategy will raise `queue.ShutDown` (caught and immediately marked completed in `submit()`), silently dropping all messages and committing their offsets without processing.

Work queues are unbounded and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`, allowing unbounded memory growth

In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each `queue.Queue()` is created with `maxsize=0` (unbounded), and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` never raises Arroyo's `MessageRejected`. Although the class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", the main consumer loop will read from Kafka at full speed and buffer an arbitrary number of `WorkItem` objects (each retaining the raw `Message` and decoded payload) in memory if any worker falls behind, risking OOM kills and also failing to flush remaining queued items on shutdown because `worker.shutdown = True` causes workers to exit their loop on the next iteration instead of draining the queue.

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before draining, dropping queued items and skipping final commit

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all workers and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run` checks `while not self.shutdown:`, any worker that finishes its current item sees `self.shutdown == True` and exits immediately instead of draining the remaining items in `work_queue` (which `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is meant to allow). Furthermore, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops `commit_thread` before calling `queue_pool.shutdown()` and never performs a final commit afterwards, so offsets for items completed during shutdown are never committed.
